newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Business leaders carve out niche in APEC.
newsitem.headline: Business leaders carve out niche in APEC.

text.p: When Bill Clinton and other Asia-Pacific leaders gather in the Philippines this month to ponder ways to free up trade, some of the hottest names in the business world will also be here chanting: "Faster, faster".
It is almost certain that the heads of government will listen.

"Not only will the business sector be formally integrated into the APEC process but a lot of their recommendations will be given cognisance not only by the ministers but by the leaders themselves," Jesus Estanislao, one of President Fidel Ramos's top advisers on APEC, said in an interview.
Ramos plays host on November 25 to the fourth annual summit of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum at Subic Bay, north of Manila.
The Philippine president has pledged to give the private sector a much higher profile this year than it got at the previous summits at Seattle, Bogor in Indonesia and Osaka.

To that end, some 400 senior executives from the region's biggest companies will also be in Manila to attend the APEC Business Forum from November 21 to 23, coinciding with a meeting of APEC foreign and trade ministers.
The companies represented range from U.S. planemaker Boeing to China's Everbright, from Japan's top conglomerates to most of the South Korean equivalent, the chaebol.
In addition, just over 50 chief executives who form the APEC Business Advisory Council have compiled a detailed list of recommendations that the APEC leaders are expected to largely endorse.

These range from the introduction of special visas for business travellers to an innovative idea for meeting Asia's massive infrastructure needs, which the World Bank has estimated at up to $1.5 trillion over the next 10 years.

Estanislao, president of Manila's University of Asia and the Pacific and a former finance minister, said the infrastructure proposal in particular was likely to be formally adopted as an APEC project.

The idea, developed by an ABAC sub-committee headed by Gordon Wu, managing director of Hong Kong's Hopewell Holdings, involves the holding of round table discussions in each economy with government agencies, private sector representatives and potential finance-providers.
The goal is to produce a list of the most important needs and start deciding how to meet them.
Over and above these recommendations, however, is a much simpler message, according to ABAC chairman Roberto Romulo, chairman of Philippine Long Distance Telephone Co and a former foreign minister.

"Let's move forward with focus and alacrity," he said, adding that the businessmen who helped make the region one of the world's most prosperous were increasingly impatient at APEC's slow pace in producing concrete results.
Romulo said in one recent interview that if private sector leaders moved as slowly as their government counterparts and produced as few results, "we'd get fired".

This year's APEC summit is expected to produce a detailed agenda for the member economies to meet their collective goal of lowering all trade and investment barriers in the region by 2010 for developed members and 2020 for the less well off.

APEC groups Australia, Brunei, Canada, Chile, China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Japan, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, the Philippines, Singapore, South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand and the United States.

Although a heightened role for the private sector is a nightmare for critics who say APEC already overwhelmingly favours big business, the executives themselves take pains to stress their social conscience.
Last month when ABAC presented its final report to President Ramos, Romulo, Wu and other CEOs said their ultimate goal was to spread prosperity throughout the region.
Wu in particular stressed the need for infrastructure such as low-cost housing in Asia's overcrowded cities. But governments and the poor should not just expect charity.
"There's no such thing as a free lunch," he added.
